title: The Farthest Reaches
author: Brett Hall
openingText: Gazing into a clear sky at night has a profound effect on many people. In some, it kindles a religious sense of wonder. In others, it sparks a curiosity about what science has so far revealed about the farthest reaches of space. Some may tend towards the spiritual. Others might study astronomy. In taking the latter path, I thought that I would come to an ever deeper understanding of the vastness of everything, the place of people in this universe, and therefore, just perhaps, what it all meant. Not because of some revelation of the ultimate and final truth, but rather a gradual unveiling; a quest through questions.
about:
The Farthest Reaches is Brett Hall's argument that people are the most important entities in the universe. Its central idea, taken from David Deutsch's The Beginning of Infinity, is explanatory universality: people are systems that can explain anything that can be explained, so there is only one kind of person and no mind exists that could understand what ours cannot. Hall, an educator and host of the ToKCast podcast, has been speaking and writing about Deutsch and Karl Popper for almost three decades, and the book grew out of a podcast series of the same name.

The preface starts from cosmology: why do people feel insignificant beside the size of the universe? Three short chapters define universality and its reach. The rest apply it, one chapter at a time, to contested questions: education and IQ, adopting a culture, immigration, ethnicity and multiculturalism, mental illness, sexuality and the trans debate, the 'woke' left and right, artificial intelligence, free speech and evolutionary psychology. In each case Hall argues that differences between people come from differences in knowledge, which can change, and not from fixed limits on the mind.

A concluding chapter is followed by Hall's commentary on an edited transcript of a 2025 conversation between Peter Boghossian and Richard Dawkins about whether some things are 'queerer than we can suppose'. An afterword addresses AI doom arguments. The writing is direct and polemical. Read for a single idea pressed into many debates, and for where you think it reaches too far or not far enough.

whyItMatters.title: One idea about what a person is
whyItMatters.body:
Hall asks what a person is and answers with a single criterion: the ability to create explanations. The book follows that criterion into education, psychology and politics to see what changes if it is true.

Today: The same question sits underneath arguments about whether AI systems could ever be people.

whyItMatters.title: Knowledge, not hardware
whyItMatters.body:
The chapters on IQ, culture and evolutionary psychology argue that differences in what people do come from what they know, not from inborn limits. Hall applies this to schooling, which he says treats students as interchangeable while sorting them by supposed ability.

Today: Debates about intelligence testing and selective education turn on this point.

whyItMatters.title: Size does not decide significance
whyItMatters.body:
The preface asks why a vast cosmos should make people feel small, and quotes Deutsch on the cow, which is larger than a person but understands nothing. The book closes by applying the same reasoning to the edge of the universe and the building blocks of matter.

Today: Cosmic pessimism appears in arguments about humanity's future; this book argues against it.

angleCards.title: Test the central claim
angleCards.text: Read Chapters 1–3 closely and state explanatory universality in your own words. Then ask what evidence or argument could show it to be false.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand explanatory universality as Brett Hall defines it in The Farthest Reaches and ask what could count against it.

angleCards.title: Follow it into the debates
angleCards.text: Choose the applied chapters closest to your interests, whether education, immigration, mental illness or AI, and judge whether the conclusion follows from the principle or from extra assumptions.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to check whether the conclusions in The Farthest Reaches's applied chapters follow from explanatory universality or depend on further assumptions.

angleCards.title: People and machines
angleCards.text: Read the chapter on artificial intelligences with the Afterword. Note how Hall separates today's AI tools from a future artificial person, and why he rejects AI doom.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Brett Hall's argument in The Farthest Reaches about the difference between current AI and artificial general intelligence.

angleCards.title: Hall and Dawkins
angleCards.text: Compare Dawkins's view that minds evolved for a 'Middle World' with Hall's claim that they can understand anything. Use the transcript and Hall's commentary.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to compare Richard Dawkins's view of the limits of the evolved mind with Brett Hall's argument for explanatory universality in The Farthest Reaches.

cast.name: Brett Hall
cast.description: An educator who hosts the podcast ToKCast and has spoken and written about the worldview of David Deutsch and Karl Popper for almost three decades. The Preface describes how studying astronomy led him to the question of what people are. The book grew from his podcast series of the same title and from public discussions with people who disagree with him.

cast.name: David Deutsch
cast.description: Oxford physicist whose book The Beginning of Infinity supplies the idea of people as 'universal explainers'. Hall calls this the deepest original insight in Deutsch's worldview and quotes him throughout, starting with the cow in the Preface.

cast.name: Karl Popper
cast.description: The philosopher whose theory of conjectural knowledge Hall says one must accept before Deutsch's account of personhood makes sense. Hall cites Popper's remark that people are equal in their infinite ignorance.

cast.name: Richard Dawkins
cast.description: The evolutionary biologist whose view that human minds evolved to understand a 'Middle World' Hall disputes. The book includes an edited 2025 conversation between Dawkins and Peter Boghossian on whether the universe is 'queerer than we can suppose', followed by Hall's reply.

cast.name: Peter Boghossian
cast.description: Philosopher who conducts the conversation with Dawkins reproduced in the book. Hall's acknowledgments thank him for helping refine the arguments about explanatory universality.

cast.name: Explanatory universality
cast.description: The claim that people can explain anything that can be explained. Hall separates the reach of people, whose ideas can transform matter on any scale, from the reach of the idea of what people are, which he applies to present-day problems.
